profile.summary: 2 Corinthians is Paul's most personal letter and presents him as a pastor in the midst of conflict. He writes to regain the church's trust in Corinth, defend his apostolic authority, and show that the gospel is revealed in reconciliation, weakness and suffering. The letter is born from a tense situation: questions about Paul, the presence of false teachers, a painful visit and a severe letter earlier, then followed by encouraging news brought by Titus. The center of the letter is that God, in Christ, reconciled sinners with him and calls his people to live in holiness, generosity and faithfulness.
profile.setting: The letter is linked to the church of Corinth, a great city, rich and influential of the Roman world, known for trade, urban prestige and social diversity. Paul was there for the first time on his second missionary journey. The environment was marked by material prosperity, intense public life and strong moral degradation, as well as religious and cultural tensions. The situation of the church reflected this context: Christians converted from a complex environment, exposed to internal disputes, criticism of leaders, influence of opponents and serious ethical problems. The most likely date of the letter is around 56 AD, after Paul left Ephesus and before his final departure to Corinth, but the composition seems linked to several stages of pastoral contact, including a previous visit and a severe letter lost today.

structure.label: Comfort amid suffering and wounded reconciliation
structure.description: Paul opens the heart on trials, afflictions and the pain caused by conflicts with Corinthian Christians, seeking to restore communion.

structure.label: The ministry of the new covenant and the power in weakness
structure.description: The apostle describes the glory of the gospel, the superiority of the new service in Christ, and the fact that the power of God appears through the fragility of the servants.

structure.label: Reconciliation in Christ and Call to Holiness
structure.description: Paul exposes the heart of the message: God has reconciled the world with him in Christ, and this requires a dedicated response from life, separated from evil.

structure.label: Response to the previous letter and instruction on generosity
structure.description: He relates the church's reaction to the disciplinary appeal, encourages joy in repentance, and teaches principles of contribution to believers in need in Jerusalem.

structure.label: Apostolic defense and confrontation with opponents
structure.description: In the final chapters, Paul directly and ironicly faces the false teachers and reaffirms their apostolic legitimacy, highlighting their weaknesses, sufferings and service.

themes: Reconciliation with God and between brothers
The power of Christ manifested in human weakness
Suffering as part of Christian Service
sacrificial genetics and care for those in need
readingKeys: Notice how Paul alternates between personal defense and pastoral exhortation, without separating his life from the content of the message.
Note the repetition of the ideas of comfort, reconciliation, weakness and glory, which structure the entire letter.
Read the passages on contribution and holiness in the light of the cross: the gospel shapes both Christian doctrine and practice.
profile.cautions: Pauline authorship is widely accepted, but the literary unit of the letter raises doubts in some excerpts. In particular, 6:14-7:1 is sometimes seen as a possible insertion or digression, and chapters 10-13 seem to respond to a later and distinct situation, perhaps linked to the emergence of new opponents. Therefore, it is prudent to read the letter acknowledging that it can gather related pastoral materials, but not necessarily written in a single moment.

dossier.narratedEra: Ambientation narrated: the life of the church in Corinth in the apostolic period, in the context of Paul's second missionary journey and its later relations with the church, already under Roman influence in Corinth and amid internal tensions in the community.
dossier.compositionEra: Composition: according to the notes, 2 Corinthians was written by Paul around A.D. 56, after his departure from Ephesus and during his stay in Macedonia, in response to the encouraging report brought by Titus and the aggravation/rescalement of disputes in Corinth. The introductions also observe academic proposals on possibly non-continuous units (especially 6:14-7:1 and 10-13), but without denying Pauline authorship.

politics.title: Corinth under Roman occupation and influence
politics.detail: The introduction describes Corinth as a city rebuilt by Julius Caesar in 44 BC and, since then, under Roman occupation and influence; from 27 BC, Acaea was under control of the Roman Senate because of the economic importance of Corinth.
politics.readingImpact: This shows that the church lived in an urban center shaped by imperial power and Roman administration; the reading of the letter should consider the environment of prestige, mobility and social pressure surrounding believers.

politics.title: Conflict of authority in Corinth
politics.detail: The notes say that the letter arose from challenges to Paul's apostolic authority and the entry of false teachers; some Corinthians questioned his leadership, and Paul had to defend his apostolate.
politics.readingImpact: The letter is not only devotional; it is also a pastoral and apologetic response to a real leadership dispute within the church.

politics.title: Rhetoric rivality and public reputation
politics.detail: Corinth is described as a city famous for its claims to wisdom and rhetoric, and opponents used Paul's weakness to depreciate his status.
politics.readingImpact: The reader must realize why Paul insists so much on weakness, cross and authenticity: his authority is not of the socially triumphant type expected in Corinthian urban culture.

politics.title: Probable scenario of persecution in Ephesus
politics.detail: In 1:8-11, the notes say that the "province of Asia" may refer to the Ephesus turmoil in Acts 19:23-41, or to a civil process at risk of execution; the source treats these possibilities as alternatives, not as certainty.
politics.readingImpact: The political background helps to read 2 Corinthians as a document born under public pressure and personal risk, reinforcing the theme of divine preservation.

politics.title: Return after Greece and possible visit to Corinth
politics.detail: The introduction states that Paul went to Macedonia, received Titus and then wrote 2 Corinthians; then he traveled to Greece, presumably Corinth, and remained three months, according to Acts 20:1-3.
politics.readingImpact: The political-missional context shows a dynamic correspondence, linked to real journeys and itinerant apostolic presence in the Roman provinces.

customs.title: Commercial city, ports and craftsmanship
customs.detail: Corinth is described as a strong economic and urban center, with shops, theaters, houses and intense commerce; artisans produced bronze, ceramics and especially known terracotta lamps in the ancient world.
customs.readingImpact: The church emerged in an environment of production and consumption, which illuminates the sensitivity of the letter to images of fragility, wealth and daily service.

customs.title: Agriculture as the basis of prosperity
customs.detail: The notes claim that agriculture was also important for Corinth's prosperity and use this to connect the city to agricultural images at 9:6-10 and 1 Color 3:6-9; 9:7,10.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to understand why Paul uses figures of sowing, harvesting and sustenance in speaking of generosity and ministry.

customs.title: Religious life and public morality
customs.detail: The introduction mentions the popularity of Aphrodite/Velyus and notes that Strabo described a large temple as a center of prostitution; however, the source also warns that scholars today are cautious about this claim by possible political rivalry between Corinth and Athens.
customs.readingImpact: The context makes the exhortation to holiness sound concrete: Paul writes to a community surrounded by religious practices and symbols that compete with Christian devotion.

customs.title: Church as mixed social group
customs.detail: Paulo's converts are described as a mixed group, an area of Corinth's cosmopolitan society, made up of people of different conditions in an environment of commerce, two ports and popular culture.
customs.readingImpact: Social diversity helps to read internal conflicts and the need for reconciliation, as the church brings together people of different backgrounds and expectations.

customs.title: Reception of letters, visits and agents as Community practice
customs.detail: The notes show that Paul wrote letters, made a personal visit, sent a severe letter with Titus and then received news through him; the church's response involved reading, welcoming and obeying apostolic letters and emissaries.
customs.readingImpact: Epistolary communication was a normal part of Christian life and explains why the letter alternates between exhortation, personal defense and relational restoration.

customs.title: Greeting with holy kiss
customs.detail: In 13:12-13, the note says that the kiss was a common Jewish form of greeting and also common practice in the New Testament church, possibly with a liturgical function of union among believers.
customs.readingImpact: The final reading of the letter must be sensitive to the community character and cult of reconciliation: communion is not only conceptual, but incarnated in concrete gestures.

language.title: Language of reconciliation and restoration
language.detail: The introduction states that the message of the good news is, above all, reconciliation, and chapter 5 is highlighted as one of the most complete exhibitions of that message (5:18-21).
language.readingImpact: This guides the reading of the whole letter: even the apostolic defense is subordinated to the ministry of reconciliation, not to Paul's personal triumph.

language.title: Weaknesses as a rhetorical and theological resource
language.detail: The notes insist that Paul was criticized for appearing weak, but that his weakness mirrors the humiliation of Christ; he ministers in weakness, but with the power of God.
language.readingImpact: The reader should interpret the autobiographical and defensive tone not as insecurity, but as a Christological re-reading of authority.

language.title: Terms of family and community affection
language.detail: In 1:8, the note points out that "brothers and sisters" translates the Greek adelphoi, a traditional term of affection for members of the same family, men and women.
language.readingImpact: This reinforces that Paul's exhortations are family and pastoral, not merely legal or administrative.

language.title: Appearance indecision and the accusation against Paul
language.detail: In 1:12-17, the notes note that Paul was accused of being voluble for changing his travel plans; the expression "sim" and "no" appears as accusation of lack of reliability.
language.readingImpact: The context explains the tone of self-defense: the credibility of the messenger and the fidelity of the message were being attacked simultaneously.

language.title: "Godous suffering" versus "the sadness of the world"
language.detail: In 7:9-10, the note distinguishes two kinds of sorrow: one leading to death and the other that produces repentance and salvation.
language.readingImpact: This distinction gives the reader a spiritual key to understanding discipline and restoration in the Corinthian church.

language.title: Brado of irony and "discourse of the madman"
language.detail: The introduction says that 10-13 contains irony, invective, ridiculous and self-defense, culminating in the so-called "Fool's Speech" (11:16"12:10).
language.readingImpact: The tone of these chapters should be read as an extreme rhetorical response to extreme opposition, not as a random change of personality.
language.reference: Introduction/The Unity of 2 Corinthians a Letter

timeline.title: First stay of Paul in Corinth
timeline.detail: The introduction places the first trip of Paul to Corinth on the second missionary journey, according to Acts 18:1-20.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone states that the letter is born from an existing missionary relationship, not occasional contact.

timeline.title: Writing of 1 Corinthians in Ephesus and the subsequent crisis
timeline.detail: The notes say that during a stay of two to three years in Ephesus (AD 53-56), Paul wrote 1 Corinthians and then faced negative reception, leading to the new crisis in Corinth.
timeline.readingImpact: This shows that 2 Corinthians responds to a concrete historical unfolding of a previous correspondence.

timeline.title: Painful visit of Paul to Corinth
timeline.detail: According to the introduction, Paul made a personal visit from Ephesus (2 Cor 2:1), but she failed to resolve the conflict and ended with humiliation and insult.
timeline.readingImpact: The letter must be read in the light of the real pastoral wound, which intensifies the request for reconciliation and trust.

timeline.title: Severe letter through Titus
timeline.detail: The introduction states that Paul then wrote a severe letter lost and sent it with Titus; 7:8-10 is read as evidence that it generated repentance.
timeline.readingImpact: This episode clarifies why 2 Corinthians alternates between relief, discipline and joy: there was a process of correction already underway.

timeline.title: Meeting with Titus in Macedonia and the essay of 2 Corinthians
timeline.detail: The source says that Paul found Titus in Macedonia and received from him an encouraging report; in response, he wrote 2 Corinthians around AD 56 and sent it back with Titus (8:6,16-19).
timeline.readingImpact: This data is important to place the tone of the letter: it mixes relief, hope and defense, because it is born of positive pastoral news but still under tension.

timeline.title: Third visit announced
timeline.detail: In 13:1-2, the note says that Paul announces his intention to go to Corinth for the third time and uses Deuteronomy 19:15 as a confirmation and judicial warning.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology helps to understand the solemnity of the closure: Paul writes as the one preparing for a decisive and disciplinary visit.

investigation: Tyndale's introduction recognizes debate about the literary unity of the letter, especially 6:14-7:1 and 10-13, but treats these issues as possibilities of interpolation, digression or subsequent composition in response to the new situation; it does not solve the problem definitively.

Matthew Henry emphasizes the two great immediate motives of the letter: the case of the incestuous man and the collection for the poor of Jerusalem; Tyndale also deals with these themes, but strongly broadens the framework of apostolic conflict and reconciliation.

Tyndale's source mentions that it cannot be known whether 10-13 corresponds to a separate letter or the final part of the same letter, and also notes that the correspondence with Corinth involved a previous lost letter.

Notes on Corinth include caution regarding Strabo's statement about the temple of Aphrodite and prostitution, recognizing possible political bias; therefore, the moral reading of the environment must remain prudent.
All dates and sequences are approximate and derived from the introductions themselves; there is no attempt here to harmonize each step with external chronologies beyond what the sources provide.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the annexed notes and, therefore, remains selective: it privileges the explicitly discussed points about Corinth, the apostolic crisis, the collection for Jerusalem, discipline and restoration, without reconstructing broader historical context from external knowledge. Some proposals appear as a debate, not as certainty, especially the literary unity of the letter, the exact identification of distress in Asia, and the extent of the alleged cult of Aphrodite. The distinction between narrated setting and date of composition was maintained: the letter speaks of Corinth's situation and Paul's missionary journey, but was later composed after the trip to Macedonia. Where notes offer several hypotheses, they have been preserved as such, without choosing beyond what the source holds.
